newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai government's rubber default rattles market.
newsitem.headline: Thai government's rubber default rattles market.

text.p: The Thai government's decision on Thursday to default on 23,100 tonnes of rubber it had bought from traders has rattled the market and could push already-low prices down further, trade and industry sources said.
Traders said although the quantity not accepted by the government was not very big, the negative impact from it could be exaggerated in a low-volume market amid bearish prices.
"With prices belly-up and ongoing currency turmoil (after an effective devaluation of the Thai baht), this is the last thing we ever expected from the government," said a trader in Hat Yai.
"I would think the prices will ease further," he told Reuters.

Thailand's natural rubber policy committee decided on Thursday not to take delivery of the rubber due this month. Deputy Prime Minister Sukavich Ransitphol who chaired the committee said the move was to cut losses as rubber prices had dropped sharply.
The government has bought more than 40,000 tonnes of RSS3 (ribbed, smoked sheet) rubber from traders for various delivery months to help prop up prices.
But weak prices forced the government to stop buying in the domestic export market since May and concentrate instead on the local spot market to please disgruntled rubber growers in the south.
The government delayed delivery of the rubber it bought to July from June before deciding to default on Thursday.
A government source said the government would stand to lose hefty amounts of money if it accepted the delivery as it had bought the rubber at around 109.00 US cents a kg.
"When the government bought, it expected to sell when the prices picked up again. But the prices has dropped by more than 20 percent since the beginning of 1997," he said.
Thai benchmark RSS3 for September delivery was offered at 95.00 US cents a kg free on board Bangkok and December at 98.00 cents on the same basis.
Another trader in Bangkok said the government's move was set to erode industry confidence in the authorities further.
"The impact of the default could be cushioned near-term by higher Tokyo values. What is more seriously at stake is government credibility," he said. --Bangkok newsroom (662) 652-0642
